account:
Today has mostly followed my appointments: morning office work and a grain inspection at the mill, lunch at home, council-letter hours, tea with my neighbour, and late-afternoon office hours. There were seventy-six hay bales at the mill stall, and no council correspondence had arrived when I asked. The unusual business is an unconfirmed report of some alteration involving the bridge or port. My secretary has been seeking firsthand accounts. The baker said he saw no alteration and only handled wheat and bread with freight and the innkeeper yesterday; he could not identify any change or its time. The secretary had not found freight at the warehouse or the innkeeper at the inn this afternoon. I therefore do not yet know whether any alteration actually occurred, much less its purpose.

My neighbour arranged an eighteen o'clock town-hall meeting, which I expressly accepted yesterday and which the secretary recorded in an appointment addendum. The neighbour described it as ordinary, said nothing urgent needed discussing beforehand, and requested no preparations or supplies. We agreed to use the great hall. I have arrived a little early, and freight, the innkeeper, and the builder are already here, apparently waiting; the builder carries a lantern. Their presence together is noteworthy, particularly because the secretary wanted to speak with two of them. It may be connected with tonight's meeting or the reported alteration, but nobody has yet told me that, so I cannot treat either connection as established. I intend to hear what they and my neighbour have to say, keeping my nineteen o'clock home appointment in mind.
